newsitem.title: USA: Espy special investigation scores two for two.
newsitem.headline: Espy special investigation scores two for two.

text.p: The legal team investigating former Agriculture Secretary Mike Espy scored another victory Wednesday, which experts said gave independent counsel Donald Smaltz an even stronger hand in his ongoing probe.

Mississippi farmer and longtime Espy political supporter Brook Keith Mitchell, along with his corporation Five M Farming Enterprises, pleaded guilty Wednesday to illegally conspiring to collect more than $700,000 in government farm payments while Espy was cabinet secretary.

The guilty plea, entered on the day Mitchell's trial was to begin, is the second successful conclusion of the second trial emerging from the govenment's more than two year investigation of the former Clinton administration official for taking illegal gifts and favours from companies his agency was in charge of regulating.

In September, Sun-Diamond Growers of California, the nation's largest fruit cooperative, was convicted on eight counts of illegally courting the favour of former Agriculture Secretary Espy by plying him with lavish gifts.

With key cases involving Espy's brother Henry and powerful Washington lobbyists still ahead, along with the continuing investigation of Mike Espy himself and corporate giant Tyson Foods, legal sources said the Mitchell plea could encourage cooperation from reluctant witnesses and arm the prosecution with important ammunition.

"This latest victory makes Smaltz appear as an able and very fearsome figure, and basically coerces all kinds of cooperation and deal making," said Georgetown University law professor Paul Rothstein. "It is good for Smaltz going into the next case ... he goes into it with a strong hand."

Smaltz's next challenge will be in New Orleans next month when a prominent law firm and the former head of the nation's largest crop insurance company go on trial on charges of money-laundering in a scheme that involved alleged illegal campaign contributions to Espy's brother Henry.

The New Orleans trial was originally set to include Henry Espy and the charges of illegal campaign contributions, but last week a federal judge in Louisiana ordered that trial be moved to Mississippi. Henry Espy is now expected to go to trial in probably the first quarter of 1997.
The investigation of Mike Espy, who resigned from the administration in 1994, is still continuing "full speed," according to sources familiar with the case.

Legal experts have said that with each victory for the prosecution, a criminal indictment of Espy looks more likely. The government is also actively investigating Arkansas-based Tyson Foods, the nation's largest poultry processor and a long supporter of President Clinton.
Sources close to the investigation said that although more indictments could be returned before year's end, the investigative phase of the case would likely continue into next year.
